front: What is WHMIS, and how does it relate to the GHS system?
back: WHMIS, the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System, is Canada's system for classifying and communicating the hazards of products used at work. Since 2015 it has been aligned with the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals, known as GHS. Nearly every product a painter uses, including thinners, primers, catalysts, strippers, and finish coats, falls under WHMIS regulation.

front: What are the three pillars WHMIS 2015 is built on?
back: WHMIS 2015 rests on three pillars: hazard classification, labelling, and safety data sheets. Hazard classification sorts products into physical hazard classes, such as flammable liquids or corrosives, and health hazard classes, such as skin irritants or carcinogens. Labels and safety data sheets then communicate those classifications to workers on the job.

front: Can a single product carry more than one WHMIS hazard classification?
back: Yes. A single can of lacquer thinner can carry more than one classification at once, for example both flammable and harmful if inhaled. Hazard classification covers both physical hazard classes, like flammable liquids, and health hazard classes, like skin irritants, and a product can fall into classes from both groups at the same time.

front: What six elements must a WHMIS 2015 label display?
back: A WHMIS 2015 label must show a product identifier, a pictogram, a signal word, hazard statements, precautionary statements, and supplier information. These six elements work together so a worker can judge a product's hazards and required precautions at a glance. Missing any of them makes a label non-compliant.

front: What is the difference between the WHMIS signal words Danger and Warning?
back: The signal word is either Danger for more severe hazards or Warning for less severe ones. Both words appear on WHMIS 2015 labels alongside the pictogram, hazard statements, and precautionary statements. The signal word gives a worker a quick sense of how serious a product's hazard is before reading further.

front: What hazard does the flame pictogram represent under WHMIS 2015?
back: The flame pictogram represents a flammable hazard. It is one of the standard WHMIS 2015 pictograms a painter must recognize, since many products such as lacquer thinner and oil based coatings are flammable. Seeing this pictogram signals a need for ignition source control and adequate ventilation.

front: What does the exclamation mark pictogram warn a painter about?
back: The exclamation mark pictogram indicates an irritant or a less severe health hazard. It represents a lower severity warning than the health hazard pictogram, which covers chronic hazards like carcinogens. A painter seeing this symbol should still take precautions such as ventilation and skin or eye protection.

front: What does the WHMIS health hazard pictogram, a figure with a starburst on the chest, indicate?
back: The health hazard pictogram shows a figure with a starburst on the chest and indicates a chronic hazard such as a carcinogen or a respiratory sensitizer. It is a more serious warning than the exclamation mark, which covers less severe irritant hazards. Isocyanate containing products are an example of materials that can carry this classification.

front: What does the WHMIS corrosion pictogram indicate?
back: The corrosion pictogram indicates a product that can cause skin or eye damage, or damage to metal. Strippers and masonry etching acids are examples of products a painter might see carrying this pictogram. Chemical splash goggles are required when handling a corrosive product that could splash into the eyes.

front: What does the WHMIS gas cylinder pictogram represent?
back: The gas cylinder pictogram represents gases under pressure. It is one of the standard WHMIS 2015 pictograms a painter must be able to identify on a label. A product carrying this pictogram requires precautions around pressurized storage and handling.

front: Is the environment pictogram legally required on WHMIS 2015 labels in Canada?
back: No, the environment pictogram is not legally required in Canada, though it is still sometimes seen on imported products. It rounds out the standard pictogram set a painter should recognize alongside the flame, exclamation mark, health hazard, corrosion, and gas cylinder pictograms. Its absence does not mean a product carries no environmental hazard.

front: What replaced the old material safety data sheet, and how is it organized?
back: Safety data sheets, or SDS, replaced the old material safety data sheets that many older tradespeople still call MSDS out of habit. An SDS follows a standardized sixteen section format covering everything from hazard identification to safe handling. This standard format lets a painter find the same type of information in the same place on any product's sheet.

front: Which SDS sections does a painter use most often, and why?
back: A painter relies most on Section 2 for hazard identification, Section 4 for first aid measures, Section 7 for safe handling and storage, Section 8 for exposure controls and required PPE, and Section 9 for physical and chemical properties. Section 9 gives flash point and vapour density, both critical when spraying in a confined space. Before applying an unfamiliar two component epoxy, the SDS is where a painter confirms ventilation requirements, the correct respirator cartridge, and first aid steps for skin contact.

front: What are a supplier's and an employer's obligations regarding an SDS?
back: A supplier must provide an SDS on request and update it within three years. The employer must keep the SDS accessible to every worker on site, not locked in an office. This lets a painter check hazard and first aid information at the point of use, not only during initial training.

front: Why is respiratory protection considered the most heavily tested piece of PPE for painters?
back: Respiratory protection is the single most misunderstood piece of PPE on a paint crew. Painters work with organic solvents, isocyanates found in polyurethane and some two component finishes, and particulates from sanding, and each hazard needs its own response rather than one respirator fitting every situation. Choosing the wrong protection for the specific hazard is a common exam trap.

front: What respirator is usually adequate for nuisance dust from sanding?
back: For nuisance dust from sanding, a properly fitted N95 or P100 particulate respirator is usually adequate. This is a lighter level of protection than what is needed for solvent vapours or isocyanates. Proper fit is essential for the respirator to filter particulates effectively.

front: What respirator protects against solvent vapours from oil based paints and thinners?
back: An air purifying respirator fitted with organic vapour cartridges, commonly identified by their black colour coding, is required for solvent vapours from oil based paints, lacquers, and most thinners. This is a step up in protection from the particulate respirator used for nuisance dust alone. The black colour coding is a quick visual check that the correct cartridge is installed.

front: How should an organic vapour cartridge's replacement schedule be decided?
back: Organic vapour cartridges have a limited service life and must be changed on a schedule based on exposure, not simply when solvent odour is noticed. Odour breakthrough often means the cartridge is already exhausted, so waiting to smell solvent is unsafe. A painter should follow a documented change schedule tied to actual exposure conditions.

front: Why are isocyanates a special respiratory concern in the coatings trade?
back: Isocyanates are a leading cause of occupational asthma in the coatings trade. Standard organic vapour cartridges do not reliably protect against isocyanate vapour and aerosol during spray application. This makes isocyanate exposure a hazard that a typical cartridge respirator cannot manage safely.

front: What respiratory protection is required when spraying two component polyurethane finishes?
back: Two component polyurethanes and many automotive style clear coats require supplied air respiration, meaning a fresh air system delivered through a hood or full face mask connected to a compressor located away from the spray zone. This is different from a cartridge respirator, which relies on filtering ambient air. Supplied air is required because the isocyanates in these coatings are not reliably filtered by cartridges.

front: On an exam, what respirator is correct for spraying a two component isocyanate product, and why?
back: In an exam scenario with a two component isocyanate product, the correct answer is supplied air, not a cartridge respirator, even a fresh one. A worker who becomes sensitized to isocyanates can react to even trace exposure afterward, so this is not a hazard to manage with a lesser level of protection. Supplied air delivers breathing air from a compressor away from the spray zone rather than filtering the air around the worker.

front: When are chemical splash goggles required instead of safety glasses?
back: Safety glasses with side shields cover general shop and site work, but chemical splash goggles are required when pouring, mixing, or spraying materials that can splash into the eyes. Strippers, masonry etching acids, and catalyzed coatings are examples of materials that require goggles. Eye protection should always be matched to the specific task being performed.

front: Does wearing a face shield remove the need for chemical splash goggles?
back: No. A face shield adds protection against larger splashes during pressure washing but does not replace goggles underneath it. A shield alone leaves the eyes open at the sides, so goggles are still needed for direct eye protection. This combination matters most during high pressure or splash prone tasks.

front: What is the everyday standard glove for brush and roller work?
back: Nitrile gloves resist a wide range of solvents and are the everyday standard for brush and roller work. They cover most day to day painting tasks where general solvent resistance is needed. Even so, nitrile is not suitable for every product a painter might handle.

front: Why can't a painter assume nitrile gloves are safe for every stripping product?
back: Aggressive solvents like methylene chloride strippers degrade nitrile quickly, so a painter should never assume one glove type covers every product on the truck. When nitrile is not adequate, the SDS will specify a more resistant glove, often neoprene or laminate. Checking the SDS before handling an aggressive stripper prevents glove failure and skin exposure.

front: At what noise level does hearing protection become mandatory for a painter?
back: Hearing protection becomes mandatory around spray equipment, compressors, and power sanding tools once noise exposure reaches regulated limits, generally around 85 decibels averaged over an eight hour shift. This is a time weighted average, not a single loud moment. Reaching this threshold triggers a mandatory hearing protection requirement on site.

front: Why can combined equipment noise exceed the hearing protection threshold even if no single tool seems loud?
back: A running compressor plus an orbital sander plus a generator on the same job can easily exceed the 85 decibel, eight hour threshold even if no single tool seems loud alone. Noise exposure adds up across every source active on site at once, not just the loudest individual tool. A painter should assess the whole work area's noise level, not judge each tool in isolation.

front: What is the four to one rule for setting up an extension ladder?
back: The four to one rule states that for every four feet of vertical height to the point of support, the base of the ladder sits one foot out from the wall. Setting the ladder steeper than this makes it prone to tipping backward, while setting it flatter lets the base slide out. Getting this ratio right is essential to a stable ladder setup.

front: How far above a landing point must an extension ladder extend, and what else is required?
back: The ladder must extend at least one metre above the landing point when stepping off onto a roof or platform. It must also be secured against movement before anyone climbs it. Both requirements protect a worker at the moment of transition between the ladder and the landing surface.

front: What are the key safety rules for using a stepladder?
back: Stepladders are rated for freestanding use only and must never be leaned against a wall. A worker should never stand on the top cap or the step below it, since doing so removes the stability the spreader bars provide. Following these limits keeps the stepladder within its designed load and stability range.

front: What are the two families of scaffolding used on a paint job?
back: Scaffolding on a paint job usually falls into two families: frame scaffold, built from prefabricated welded frames stacked and cross braced, and system scaffold, using a modular ring or cup lock connection. Both systems serve the same purpose of building a stable elevated working platform. The choice between them depends on the job and the equipment available.

front: What base conditions must scaffolding sit on before it is built up?
back: Scaffolding must sit on a stable, level base, using base plates or screw jacks on uneven ground. This applies to both frame scaffold and system scaffold. A poorly prepared base undermines the stability of the entire structure no matter how well the frames above it are assembled.

front: At what platform height must scaffolding be fully planked with guardrails?
back: Scaffolding must be fully planked with guardrails once a working platform exceeds the height threshold set by the applicable provincial regulation, typically around three metres, though thresholds do vary by province. A painter should confirm the exact local threshold rather than assuming it is the same everywhere in Canada. Below that threshold, requirements may be less strict, but they still apply once the limit is reached.

front: What rules apply to the wheels of a mobile scaffold tower?
back: Mobile scaffold towers add wheels with locking casters, which must always be locked before anyone climbs. The tower must never be moved while a worker is still on the platform. These rules prevent the tower from shifting or rolling while it is bearing a worker's weight at height.

front: Why must a swing stage's fall arrest lifeline be independent of its suspension ropes?
back: Swing stages and suspended platforms require workers to wear a full body harness connected to an independent fall arrest lifeline at all times, completely separate from the suspension ropes holding the stage itself. This independence is the point tested most often on the exam. The fall arrest system must function even if the primary suspension fails, which is exactly why it cannot share the same ropes.

front: What are the three core components of a personal fall arrest system?
back: A personal fall arrest system has three core components: a full body harness, a connecting device such as a shock absorbing lanyard or self retracting lifeline, and an anchor point rated to the load the system could impose in a fall. All three components must work together correctly for the system to arrest a fall safely. Missing or substituting any one component compromises the whole system.

front: What is the minimum anchor point rating for a personal fall arrest system under most Canadian standards?
back: An anchor point must be rated to the load the system could impose in a fall, typically a minimum of twenty two kilonewtons per worker under most Canadian standards. The anchor point must also limit both the fall distance and any swing fall hazard. A weak or improperly rated anchor point undermines the entire fall arrest system regardless of harness quality.

front: What factors go into calculating the total fall clearance needed below a work surface?
back: Total fall clearance accounts for lanyard length, deceleration distance, and harness stretch. Workers must know this total clearance so they do not strike a lower level before the fall arrest system fully arrests the fall. Underestimating any one of these factors can leave insufficient clearance even with a properly rated anchor point.

front: What three elements make up a compliant guardrail system?
back: A guardrail system needs a top rail at the height specified by the applicable regulation, a mid rail, and toe boards where tools or material could fall on workers below. Guardrail systems are used as an alternative to personal fall arrest equipment. All three elements work together to prevent both falls and falling objects.

front: Why must every fall arrest plan include a rescue procedure, not just fall prevention equipment?
back: Working at heights training, now mandatory in several provinces, covers hazard recognition, equipment inspection, and rescue planning. A worker suspended in a harness can develop suspension trauma within minutes if not rescued promptly. Because of this, every fall arrest plan must include a rescue procedure and cannot rely on equipment alone to keep a fallen worker safe.

front: Why are natural bristle brushes limited to oil based and alkyd coatings?
back: Water causes natural bristles to swell and lose their shape, so natural bristle brushes are reserved for oil based and alkyd coatings only. Synthetic filament brushes, usually a nylon and polyester blend, handle both latex and oil based products and are the standard general purpose choice today.

front: Describe the correct steps to clean a brush after using latex paint.
back: Work warm water and a mild detergent through the bristles from heel to tip, then comb the filaments to realign them and wrap the brush in brown paper to dry in shape. Cleaning should start immediately after use, before material dries in the ferrule, since a brush left unshaped or resting on its bristles develops a permanent curl or splayed tip.

front: What extra step does cleaning an oil based paint brush require beyond solvent?
back: After working mineral spirits or the solvent specified on the label through the bristles, the brush needs a final wash in soap and water to remove residual solvent. It is then combed to realign the filaments and wrapped in brown paper to dry in shape, the same finishing steps used for a latex brush.

front: How should a roller cover be reused after latex work, and how should it dry?
back: Spin or roll the cover dry on scrap material to remove excess paint, then rinse it under water while working the nap by hand until the water runs clear. The cover should be hung to dry rather than left standing on its end, since standing flattens the nap and ruins the finish it produces.

front: Are oil based roller covers typically cleaned and reused? Explain the trade reasoning.
back: No, roller covers used with oil based coatings are usually treated as disposable. The cost of solvent and the labour needed to clean an oil based cover properly is generally not worth it compared to simply replacing the cover for the next job.

front: List the steps for flushing an airless sprayer at the end of a work session.
back: Relieve the system pressure, remove and clean the tip and tip guard, then run the appropriate flushing fluid through the system until it runs clear, water for latex or mineral spirits or the specified solvent for oil based and catalyzed coatings. If the sprayer will sit idle for more than a day or two, run a pump armor or storage fluid through it, since dried paint inside a pump can permanently damage seals and packing.

front: Why do spray tips need periodic replacement, and how is wear identified?
back: The abrasive action of pigment passing through a spray tip gradually wears and enlarges the orifice, which changes the fan pattern. Tips should be checked against a wear gauge and replaced once the spray pattern becomes tailed or uneven.

front: What two problems result from an extension pole that flexes excessively under load?
back: An excessively flexing extension pole is both a quality problem and a safety problem, since it can affect the cut and finish while a worker applies pressure overhead. It can also slip or break unexpectedly, so poles should be checked for a secure, non slipping tool end connection and stored fully retracted to prevent bent sections.

front: How is the paintable area of a plain rectangular wall calculated?
back: Multiply the wall's height by its width to get the area in square metres or square feet. Windows, doors, and any other openings that will not be painted are then subtracted from that figure to arrive at the true paintable area.

front: How is the area of a triangular gable end calculated for estimating?
back: Multiply the base of the gable by its height, then divide the result by two, the standard formula for the area of a triangle. This figure is added to the estimate separately from the rectangular wall sections below it.

front: What formula gives the paintable area of a ceiling?
back: Ceiling area is calculated by multiplying the room's length by the room's width, the same basic rectangular area formula used for a flat surface. This figure is combined with the wall and any triangular areas to reach the total paintable area for the space.

front: After finding total paintable area, what two divisions convert it into litres or gallons of paint needed?
back: Divide the total paintable area by the coating's stated coverage rate, commonly expressed as square metres per litre or square feet per gallon, then divide that result again by the number of coats specified. A two coat system needs roughly double the amount calculated for a single coat, so both divisions must be applied before ordering material.

front: What waste allowance does a competent estimator typically add to a paint quantity, and why?
back: A competent estimator adds an allowance for surface porosity and waste, typically an extra ten percent, on top of the calculated coverage figure. Porous surfaces absorb more coating than the manufacturer's stated rate assumes, and some product is always lost to spillage, tray residue, and application loss.

front: What is the approximate volume of one imperial gallon in litres?
back: One imperial gallon equals roughly 4.55 litres. Confusing the imperial gallon with the US gallon produces a material shortfall, since paint manufacturers list their coverage rate against a specific gallon size.

front: Which gallon size is most commonly sold in Canadian retail, and what is it in litres?
back: The US gallon, equal to roughly 3.785 litres, is the size most commonly sold in Canadian retail even though Canada is a metric country. A painter needs to know which gallon size a product's stated coverage rate is based on, since mixing up the imperial and US gallon leads to ordering the wrong quantity.

front: A two component epoxy specifies a four to one mixing ratio by volume. What does that mean?
back: Four parts of the base component are combined with one part of the hardener component, and that proportion must be scaled up or down exactly no matter what total volume is being mixed. An incorrect ratio can leave the cured coating soft, tacky, or brittle, so the four to one relationship must never drift.

front: A product label allows a maximum ten percent thinning by volume. How much thinner may be added to ten litres of paint?
back: No more than one litre of thinner may be added to ten litres of paint under a maximum ten percent by volume limit. Exceeding that limit affects film build, drying time, and adhesion, and it can also push the coating's VOC content above what the label and regulation allow.

front: How does a mixing ratio differ from a maximum thinning percentage in trade math terms?
back: A mixing ratio, such as four to one for a two component epoxy, is a fixed proportion between two components that must be scaled up or down exactly to work at all. A maximum thinning percentage, such as ten percent, is an upper limit on how much thinner may be added to a single component product, where staying under the limit is fine but exceeding it causes problems with film build, drying time, and adhesion.

front: Under the Construction Specifications Canada Masterformat system, which division covers painting work?
back: Painting typically falls under division 09 of the Construction Specifications Canada, or CSC, Masterformat system used to organize commercial and institutional project specifications. A painter working from a Masterformat spec looks to division 09 for the products, film thickness, and coat count required.

front: What kinds of information does a commercial painting specification typically call out?
back: A specification names the exact products to be used, the required film thickness, the number of coats, and the surface preparation standard, sometimes referencing an external standard such as an SSPC grade for steel. Following the spec exactly matters because owners expect the specified system to be applied, not a painter's own familiar substitution.

front: What risk does a painter take by substituting their own familiar system in place of the written specification?
back: Ignoring the written spec in favour of a personal system risks a failed inspection and a costly redo, since the owner expects the specified system to be applied. Any substitution needs formal written approval before it is used, not just the painter's own judgment on site.

front: How does a painter use a project's room finish schedule during a commercial job?
back: The painter cross references the finish schedule against the actual space to confirm which coating system each surface receives, since a single project can specify different finishes room by room. For example, a project might call for an eggshell finish in office areas, a semi gloss in washrooms, and an epoxy system in a mechanical room.

front: Why is a residential work order considered a legal record, and what happens if work goes beyond it?
back: A work order specifying colour, sheen, brand, and included rooms is the legal record of what the painter and customer agreed to. Completing work outside that documented scope without written change authorization creates disputes over payment, since neither party has a signed record of the extra work being approved.

front: How are VOC limits for coatings measured, and do they vary across Canada?
back: Volatile organic compound limits restrict how much VOC a coating may contain, measured in grams per litre. These limits vary both by product category and by province, with some provinces adopting stricter limits than the federal baseline.

front: How can the recoat behaviour of low and zero VOC coatings differ from older solvent heavy products?
back: Low VOC and zero VOC coatings, now the dominant category for interior work, can behave differently from older solvent heavy formulations. Their recoat restrictions are often tied to humidity and temperature rather than to solvent flash off, so a painter cannot rely on old solvent based timing rules.

front: On what basis should a painter presume a building may contain lead based paint?
back: Any building constructed or last painted before 1980 should be presumed to have lead based paint, since lead was commonly used in residential paint until it was phased out through the 1970s. Before sanding, scraping, or heat stripping old paint on a pre-1980s structure, the painter should test the coating or treat it as presumed lead containing.

front: What lead safe work practices apply once old paint on a pre-1980s building is disturbed?
back: Lead safe work practices include containment of the work area, wet methods or HEPA filtered sanding rather than dry sanding, respiratory protection rated for lead particulate, and disposal of paint chips and dust as hazardous waste. These controls apply whether the paint is confirmed to contain lead or only presumed to, since testing is not always done first.

front: Why is dry sanding or open flame stripping of suspected lead paint treated as a serious violation?
back: Dry sanding or open flame stripping of suspected lead paint without containment, wet or HEPA methods, and proper respiratory protection is both a regulatory violation and a genuine health hazard. The risk is particularly serious for children and pregnant workers near a residential site, since lead dust and fume can spread well beyond the immediate work area.

front: Can leftover liquid paint waste and used solvents go into a regular waste bin?
back: No, liquid paint waste, used solvents, and containers still carrying a hazardous residue cannot go into a regular waste bin in any province. They fall under hazardous waste rules that require proper handling and disposal instead.

front: What is the difference between disposing of consumer paint quantities and contractor quantities of hazardous liquid waste?
back: Most provinces run a paint stewardship program that allows dropoff of leftover consumer paint at approved depots. Contractor quantities of hazardous liquid waste are larger and require proper manifesting and pickup by a licensed carrier rather than a simple depot dropoff.

front: Why must oily rags be stored in a sealed metal container rather than left piled up?
back: Oily rags present a spontaneous combustion risk if they are piled together, since the oxidation of the oil trapped in the fabric can generate enough heat to ignite the pile without any outside flame. They must be stored in a sealed metal container until proper disposal, a detail tested as a fire prevention question as often as an environmental one.

front: State the relationship between wet film thickness, percent volume solids, and dry film thickness.
back: Wet film thickness multiplied by percent volume solids equals dry film thickness, since only the solid portion of the coating remains once the carrier evaporates. This relationship lets a painter predict the final dry film build directly from the wet film reading taken during application.

front: A coating is 50% volume solids and applied at a 200 micrometre wet film thickness. What dry film thickness results?
back: The resulting dry film thickness is roughly 100 micrometres, since 200 micrometres × 50% volume solids equals 100 micrometres. Only the solid portion of the applied coating remains behind after the liquid carrier evaporates.

front: What should a painter's daily records note for exterior work, and why does it matter later?
back: Daily records for exterior work should note weather conditions, since temperature and humidity affect cure and recoat windows during application. This record can matter later if a warranty claim is made, since it documents whether conditions at the time of application met the product's requirements.

front: Why should material batch numbers be logged on a large painting job?
back: Logging material batch numbers on large jobs allows a colour or performance issue to be traced back to its source if a problem shows up later. Without that record, it becomes far harder to determine whether a defect came from a specific batch of product or from the application itself.

front: What must happen in writing before extra work proceeds beyond the original scope?
back: A change order needs to be documented in writing before extra work proceeds, protecting both the painter and the client from disputes over scope and payment. Verbal agreement to extra work is not enough of a record if a disagreement arises later.

front: What customer service practices help a painter set realistic expectations and avoid complaints on a job?
back: Clear communication about the scope of work, the timeline, and how furnishings will be protected sets realistic expectations for the customer before work begins. This kind of upfront communication heads off complaints that arise when a customer's assumptions do not match what was actually agreed to.

front: On a commercial site, what does professional communication extend to beyond the customer relationship?
back: On a commercial site, professional communication extends to coordinating with other trades and respecting the site's safety orientations. A painter is also expected to report hazards or near misses through the proper reporting channel rather than mentioning them informally.

front: Why should hazards or near misses on a commercial site be reported through the proper channel?
back: Reporting hazards or near misses through the proper channel gets the information to whoever is responsible for site safety, so it can be tracked and acted on. An informal mention to a coworker does not create the record or trigger the response that a proper report does.

front: Why does professional conduct in this trade get judged as much by paperwork as by finish quality?
back: A journeyperson's professional conduct is judged as much by paperwork and communication, daily records, batch numbers, and documented change orders, as by the quality of the finished coating. Careful records protect the painter from disputes and provide evidence if a warranty claim or scope disagreement arises later.

front: What causes the blotchy "flashing" look on new drywall, and how is it prevented?
back: Flashing happens when joint compound, screw patches, and paper facing absorb paint at different rates because the drywall is porous and unsealed. A PVA drywall primer seals the whole surface evenly first, so the topcoat is absorbed at the same rate everywhere and the sheen looks uniform.

front: Why does fresh plaster need weeks to cure before coating, and what happens if you coat it too soon?
back: Plaster is denser and more alkaline than drywall, and lime plaster in particular can take weeks to fully cure. Coating it too soon traps residual moisture and alkaline salts underneath the film, which can blister or saponify an oil-based finish.

front: How should a painter distinguish a cosmetic plaster crack from ongoing structural movement?
back: A cosmetic hairline crack is stable and stays filled once repaired properly. A structural crack keeps reopening no matter how well it is filled, because the building movement causing it has not stopped, so the underlying cause needs addressing before the surface repair will hold.

front: What is mill glaze on new wood, and why must it be removed before coating?
back: Mill glaze is a burnished surface left on kiln-dried lumber, millwork, or trim by the planing process. It resists absorption, so new wood must be sanded to remove it, in addition to being moisture-checked and having knots or resinous areas treated so sap does not bleed through.

front: When assessing previously painted wood, what age threshold requires checking for lead paint in Canada?
back: Any structure built before 1990 in Canada must be checked for lead paint before old film is removed. Beyond that check, the painter also assesses how well the existing coating is adhered and decides whether it needs full removal or can simply be feathered and recoated.

front: How long can fresh concrete or stucco take to fully cure, and what happens if it is coated too early?
back: Fresh concrete typically needs a recommended cure period of about a month, commonly 28 days, before it is ready to coat, while fresh stucco cures much more slowly and can take up to a year to fully cure. Coating either before alkalinity drops and moisture escapes causes efflorescence, a white powdery salt deposit, to push through the applied film.

front: Why must bare ferrous metal always be primed before topcoating?
back: Ferrous metal, meaning iron and steel, is the substrate most vulnerable to corrosion. Left bare, it starts oxidizing again almost immediately, so it must be primed with a rust-inhibitive primer before any topcoat is applied.

front: How does non-ferrous metal like aluminum and galvanized steel corrode differently from ferrous metal?
back: Non-ferrous metal does not rust the way iron or steel does, but it still oxidizes on the surface. Aluminum forms an oxide layer, while galvanized steel develops zinc oxide, commonly called white rust, and that surface layer must be addressed or a new coating will peel off.

front: Why can fresh galvanizing be a problem for coating adhesion?
back: Fresh galvanizing is too smooth for most primers to grip properly. A galvanized-specific primer or a weathering period is needed before coating, so the surface either has the right chemistry to bond or enough time to develop a texture a standard primer can hold onto.

front: What pressure range is used for pressure washing wood siding and stucco, and why?
back: Wood siding and stucco are typically washed at lower pressure, often 1200 to 1800 psi, using a wide fan tip. Excessive pressure can etch wood fibres, drive water behind the siding, or blast mortar out of masonry joints.

front: How long should you generally let a pressure-washed exterior surface dry before coating begins?
back: After pressure washing, a common drying period is 24 to 48 hours before coating starts. This allows surface and near-surface moisture to escape so the new film is not applied over a substrate that is still wet.

front: When is hand washing preferred over pressure washing for cleaning a substrate?
back: Hand washing with a sponge, brush, or cloth is used where pressure washing risks damage, such as on delicate trim or older, softer mortar. It is slower than pressure washing, but it gives direct control and lets a painter feel for soft, deteriorated material while cleaning.

front: What is TSP, and why have many crews switched to phosphate-free substitutes?
back: TSP is trisodium phosphate, a heavy-duty cleaner and degreaser that cuts through grease and grime while lightly etching glossy surfaces to improve adhesion. Because it is phosphate-based, many provinces restrict it over phosphate runoff into waterways, so most crews now use phosphate-free substitutes formulated to do the same job.

front: Why must a surface be rinsed thoroughly after cleaning with TSP or a phosphate-free substitute?
back: Leftover cleaner residue on the surface interferes with the new coating's adhesion. A thorough rinse after cleaning removes that residue so the primer and topcoat can bond properly to the substrate underneath.

front: Where is degreasing especially critical before coating, and why won't a general cleaner do the job?
back: Degreasing is critical in kitchens, mechanical rooms, garages, and commercial spaces where airborne grease settles over time. A general-purpose cleaner will not fully remove that grease film, so a dedicated degreaser formulated for the purpose is needed.

front: What is the water-break test, and what does it tell a painter?
back: In a water-break test, water is applied to a cleaned surface: if grease film remains, the water beads up instead of sheeting evenly across it. Beading tells the painter that cleaning is not yet finished and more degreasing is needed.

front: How should mildew and algae be treated, and why is this different from ordinary dirt removal?
back: Mildew and algae are biological growth, not dirt, so they need a diluted bleach solution or a dedicated mildewcide, followed by a thorough rinse, rather than just cleaning. Killing the organism is required, since simply washing away visible growth without treating it leaves it able to keep growing.

front: What happens if a painter coats over mildew without killing it first?
back: The organism keeps growing underneath the new film and telegraphs back through the coating as staining, usually within a season. This is a common cause of early exterior coating failure, which is why shaded, damp areas prone to recurring growth often need a mildew-resistant additive or coating.

front: How should a scraper blade be held when removing peeling or flaking paint?
back: A stiff-bladed scraper is held at an angle low enough to lift loose material without gouging the sound wood or plaster underneath. The edge of intact paint should be feathered so there is no hard ridge for the new coating to telegraph through.

front: What is the approximate grit range for coarse sandpaper, and what is it used for?
back: Coarse grits, roughly 60 to 80, remove material quickly and are used for aggressive stripping. They leave deep scratches in the surface that must be refined with finer grits afterward before the surface is ready for priming.

front: What grit range is considered the workhorse range for general surface prep sanding?
back: Medium grits, roughly 100 to 150, are the workhorse range for general prep. They smooth the surface further than a coarse grit while still working efficiently, and are typically used between an initial coarse pass and the final fine sanding.

front: What grit range is used for final smoothing immediately before priming?
back: Fine grits, roughly 180 to 220, are used for final smoothing before priming. At this stage the goal is a smooth, even surface rather than material removal, so the substrate is ready to accept the primer coat cleanly.

front: Why must sanding progress from coarse grit to fine grit in stages, rather than starting with fine grit alone?
back: Fine grit alone cannot remove the scratch pattern that a coarser grit leaves behind. Sanding must move from coarse to fine so each finer grit refines and removes the marks left by the grit before it, ending in a smooth, evenly prepared surface.

front: When is hand sanding preferred over power sanding, and when is power sanding standard practice?
back: Hand sanding gives more control and suits delicate work, tight corners, and fine finish work where power tools risk removing too much material too fast. Power sanding covers large areas far faster and is standard for exterior siding and large drywall repairs, though it demands care to avoid swirl marks or sanding through a veneer.

front: What is wire brushing used for, and what tools does it involve?
back: Wire brushing is used on metal and masonry to remove loose rust, mill scale, and old failing paint down to sound base material. A hand wire brush suits small areas, while a power wire wheel or cup brush mounted on a drill or grinder covers larger areas much faster.

front: How soon should freshly wire-brushed bare steel be primed, and why?
back: Freshly wire-brushed bare steel should be primed as soon as practical. Exposed steel begins oxidizing again almost immediately, so leaving it bare too long after brushing undoes the benefit of the prep work.

front: What kind of repairs is spackle designed for, and what are its limits?
back: Spackle is a lightweight, quick-drying filler suited to small interior repairs such as nail holes and minor dents in drywall or plaster. It shrinks minimally and sands easily, but it is not intended for structural gaps or large voids.

front: What is the difference between setting-type and drying-type joint compound?
back: Setting-type joint compound hardens through a chemical reaction and can be recoated the same day. Drying-type compound cures as water evaporates from it, which takes longer, though it sands more easily once it has fully dried.

front: Why is setting-type joint compound usually the better choice for deep drywall fills?
back: Setting-type compound will not shrink and crack the way a thick application of drying-type compound can. Because drying-type compound cures by evaporation, a deep fill of it is prone to shrinking as it dries, which is more likely to crack.

front: What is the difference between solvent-based and water-based wood filler?
back: Solvent-based wood fillers sand to a hard, smooth finish and suit stain-grade work. Water-based fillers clean up more easily and are typically used under paint rather than stain, since they may not take stain evenly.

front: What makes epoxy filler suited to exterior wood repairs like rotted sills and jambs?
back: Epoxy fillers are two-part systems that cure to an extremely hard, durable patch, will not shrink, and resist moisture once cured. They can also be shaped to match the surrounding profile, though they cost more and take more labour, so they are reserved for exterior-grade repairs rather than everyday touch-ups.

front: How should a painter choose which filling compound to use for a given repair?
back: The material should match the job: sandable fillers like spackle for small blemishes, setting-type compound for larger drywall repairs, wood filler for wood-specific defects, and epoxy for anything exterior or exposed to ongoing moisture. Matching filler to substrate and exposure prevents an early repeat failure of the repair.

front: What are the main properties and limits of acrylic latex caulk?
back: Acrylic latex caulk is the most common general-purpose caulk, paintable almost immediately, cleans up with water, and suits interior trim, baseboards, and moderate gaps. It has less flexibility and durability than silicone or polyurethane, making it a poor choice for constantly moving joints or high-moisture exterior locations.

front: Why is standard silicone caulk limited for use on trim and siding despite its water resistance?
back: Silicone caulk offers excellent flexibility, adhesion, and water resistance, making it standard around tubs, sinks, and wet areas. Standard silicone is not paintable, which limits its use on trim and siding, so specialty paintable silicone and silicone-modified acrylic hybrids exist to bridge that gap.

front: Why is polyurethane caulk commonly chosen for exterior joints with significant thermal movement?
back: Polyurethane caulk offers strong adhesion, high flexibility, and excellent durability against weather and movement. It is paintable, but it has a longer cure time and a stronger odour than acrylic latex, and it should not be used against other sealants without checking compatibility.

front: Why is backer rod used in a wide gap before caulking, rather than just filling it with caulk directly?
back: Foam backer rod fills a gap too wide to bridge properly, so the caulk bonds on two sides only rather than three. Bonding on two sides lets the bead flex properly as the joint moves, instead of being rigidly anchored across the whole gap.

front: What happens to a caulk bead that ends up bonded across three surfaces instead of two?
back: A bead applied across three bonding surfaces tears at the centre under normal movement instead of stretching. This is why backer rod is used in wide gaps, so the caulk only bonds to the two sides of the joint and can flex as intended.

front: Why is tooling a caulk bead an important finishing step?
back: Tooling the bead with a wet finger, caulking tool, or damp rag smooths it into a consistent, slightly concave profile and removes excess for a clean line. A properly tooled bead sheds water better and looks far more professional than one left straight from the tube.

front: What is PVA primer used for, and what is it not suited to?
back: PVA primer, often called drywall primer, seals new drywall evenly so paper facing, joint compound, and screw patches absorb the topcoat at the same rate, preventing flashing. It is not intended for exterior use or stain blocking.

front: What does wood primer typically contain to address woods like cedar and redwood?
back: Wood primer is formulated for adhesion and flexibility on wood and typically contains additives to block tannin bleed from woods like cedar and redwood. Oil-based versions penetrate and seal raw or weathered wood well, while water-based versions offer lower odour and faster dry time.

front: What problem does masonry primer address that a standard primer cannot handle?
back: Masonry primer, often called an alkali-resistant or masonry conditioner primer, is designed for the high alkalinity and porosity of concrete, stucco, and masonry. It penetrates and binds a chalky surface and resists breakdown from residual alkalinity, which would otherwise saponify an unsuitable coating.

front: Why does bare ferrous metal specifically require a rust-inhibitive primer?
back: Rust-inhibitive metal primers contain corrosion-inhibiting pigments and bond tightly to bare steel or iron, forming a barrier against moisture and oxygen. Without this barrier, bare ferrous metal starts oxidizing again almost immediately, undermining any topcoat applied over it.

front: Why can a standard steel primer be the wrong choice for aluminum or galvanized steel?
back: Non-ferrous metals like aluminum and galvanized steel need a primer formulated specifically for that substrate, since a standard steel primer may not adhere properly to it. Choosing the wrong primer chemistry for the metal type risks early adhesion failure of the whole coating system.

front: What kind of substrate contaminants call for a stain-blocking primer, and how does it work?
back: Stain-blocking primer is used wherever a substrate carries a contaminant that would otherwise bleed through, such as water stains, smoke or nicotine staining, marker or ink, and knots or tannin-rich wood. These are typically shellac-based or specially formulated products that seal in the stain rather than simply covering it.

front: When is spot priming appropriate, and when does a job require full priming instead?
back: Spot priming, applying primer only on repaired areas, bare wood, or stains, is appropriate when the existing painted surface is otherwise sound, clean, and well adhered. Full priming is required on new substrates, when changing coating types, when there is extensive bare or repaired area, or when the existing finish's condition is too questionable to assume uniform adhesion.

front: What is a common source of uneven sheen or early coating failure related to priming decisions?
back: Choosing spot priming on a surface that actually needed full priming is a common source of uneven sheen or early failure. This mistake happens when a painter assumes an existing finish is sound and uniformly adhered without properly checking its condition first.

front: What is the difference between a pin-type and a pinless moisture meter?
back: A pin-type moisture meter measures resistance between two probes inserted into the material. A pinless moisture meter uses electromagnetic sensing across the surface instead, so it can check moisture content without puncturing the substrate.

front: What moisture content range is generally acceptable in wood before coating?
back: For wood, acceptable moisture content before coating generally falls in the 12 to 15 percent range, with finish-grade millwork expected closer to the lower end. Checking with a moisture meter rather than guessing avoids coating over wood that is still too wet.

front: What moisture content is typically acceptable for concrete, masonry, and stucco before coating?
back: For concrete, masonry, and stucco, acceptable moisture content is typically under about 12 percent. New concrete and stucco should also cure for the recommended period regardless of a surface reading, since alkalinity and deep moisture can persist even when the surface tests dry.

front: What are the recommended cure periods for new concrete and new stucco before coating?
back: New concrete commonly needs a recommended cure period of 28 days, while new stucco can need up to a year. Both periods apply regardless of a surface moisture reading, since deep moisture and alkalinity can persist below a surface that already tests dry.

front: How can a painter get a rough field indication of substrate moisture without a moisture meter?
back: A plastic sheet taped to the surface and checked for condensation after 24 hours gives a rough field indication of moisture. Condensation forming under the sheet suggests the substrate is releasing moisture and is not yet ready to coat.

front: What happens when a coating is applied over a substrate with excess moisture?
back: Coating over excess moisture traps it behind a film that is often less permeable than the substrate itself. As the trapped moisture tries to escape, it pushes the coating up from underneath, producing blistering, and in freeze-thaw climates it can also drive spalling in masonry.

front: What is peeling, and what are its typical causes and fix?
back: Peeling is separation and lifting of a coating from the substrate or a previous coat, usually in sheets or curls. It is usually caused by moisture behind the film, poor prep before the last coating, or incompatibility between layers, and the fix is to scrape back to sound material, address any moisture source, and prime before recoating.

front: What is chalking, and how does its treatment differ between light and heavy cases?
back: Chalking is a powdery, dusty residue on an aged coating, especially common on exterior paints exposed to prolonged UV, where the binder breaks down and releases pigment as loose powder. Light chalking can sometimes be cleaned and coated over after thorough washing and an adhesion test, but heavy chalking needs removal by scrubbing, pressure washing, or mechanical abrasion, often followed by a binding primer.

front: What is alligatoring, and why can it generally not be spot-repaired?
back: Alligatoring is a pattern of deep, interconnected cracks resembling reptile skin, typically caused by an aged, brittle coating, often oil-based, losing flexibility over years. Because the cracking runs through multiple layers, it generally cannot be spot-repaired and needs to be removed to a sound layer by scraping and sanding the full area before priming and recoating.

front: How does cracking differ from alligatoring, and what causes it?
back: Cracking refers to linear or hairline cracks in the film, distinct from the deep, interconnected pattern of alligatoring. It results from a coating applied too thick, applied in unsuitable temperatures, or simple aging and movement, and fine cracking may be handled by sanding and priming the area.

front: What causes blistering in a paint film, and how should it be repaired?
back: Blistering is the formation of bubbles in the film, caused mainly by moisture trapped beneath the coating or by painting over a contaminated surface. Blisters need to be scraped off completely, the underlying cause corrected, and the area properly primed before recoating, since sanding a blister smooth without fixing the cause will see it return.

front: What are the basic steps for containing dust when sanding drywall or plaster indoors?
back: Basic containment starts with isolating the work area using plastic sheeting over doorways and openings, taped securely to stop dust migrating into occupied spaces, along with covering furniture that will not be worked on. Negative air setups, a fan exhausting through a filtered opening to the exterior, pull dust out of the work zone and are standard on larger commercial jobs.

front: Why is dust collection at the tool considered more effective than cleaning up dust afterward?
back: Dust collection attached directly at the tool, whether a sander with a vacuum port or a shop vacuum with a HEPA filter, captures dust at the source before it becomes airborne. A true HEPA filter matters because standard filters pass fine particulate straight through, and that fine dust is most likely to be inhaled.

front: Why is wet wiping preferred over dry sweeping when cleaning up sanding dust?
back: Dry sweeping re-suspends dust back into the air instead of removing it. Wet wiping surfaces, along with regular vacuum cleanup through the day and proper disposal of collected dust, reduces the amount of airborne dust and keeps the work area clean, which clients notice on occupied residential jobs.

front: Why is the age of a building the key screening question for lead-based paint risk, not the paint's appearance?
back: Lead was a common paint additive in Canada until federal regulations began restricting it in consumer paint in the late 1970s, so any building constructed or last painted before 1980 should be treated as a probable lead risk until proven otherwise. A coat that looks perfectly sound can still contain lead, while chipping, alligatored paint may test clean, so a painter should never judge lead risk by eye alone.

front: What should a painter do first when facing a suspect lead-painted surface, before any sanding or scraping?
back: A painter's first move on a suspect surface is testing, not sanding. Confirming or ruling out lead before disturbing the surface prevents releasing airborne lead dust unnecessarily and determines which safe work practices apply.

front: What are rhodizonate test kits used for, and what is their key limitation?
back: Rhodizonate chemistry test kits give a quick colour-change result on site, useful for a first pass at screening a surface for lead. They are not always reliable on darker or multi-layer paint films, so results need to be interpreted with caution on those surfaces.

front: When is sending a paint chip sample to an accredited lab preferred over an on-site test kit?
back: Where certainty matters, a paint chip sample sent to an accredited lab gives a defensible result, unlike a quick on-site colour-change kit. This is the more reliable route when a definite answer is required rather than a fast first pass.

front: Should a negative result from a cheap lead swab kit override the pre-1980 presumption of lead risk?
back: No. A negative result from a cheap swab kit should never override common sense on a pre-1980 building. When in doubt on an older structure, the surface should still be treated as positive for lead.

front: Describe the encapsulation strategy for dealing with confirmed lead-based paint.
back: Encapsulation seals the existing lead paint under a bonding coating designed to stay intact without cracking. It is often the most practical choice on sound, well-adhered paint, since it controls the hazard without disturbing the paint film underneath.

front: Describe the enclosure strategy for dealing with lead-based paint, with an example.
back: Enclosure covers the surface entirely with a new rigid material, such as installing drywall over old plaster, isolating the lead paint rather than removing it. The lead hazard remains in place but is permanently sealed behind the new surface.

front: When is full removal chosen as a lead abatement strategy, and what risk does it carry?
back: Removal, by wet hand scraping, chemical stripping, or HEPA-vacuum sanding tools, is reserved for situations where the substrate must return to bare material. Of the three lead abatement strategies it produces the highest waste volume and the greatest exposure risk.

front: Which methods are prohibited on suspect lead-based paint, and why are they banned?
back: Dry sanding, dry scraping, and open-flame torching of suspect lead paint are prohibited because they release airborne lead dust and fumes. Approved methods instead keep the paint wet or use a HEPA-filtered vacuum shroud on the tool to capture debris as it is created.

front: Describe the wet scraping technique used on a small lead paint removal job.
back: Wet scraping mists the surface immediately ahead of the scraper blade as the painter works, keeping lead dust from becoming airborne. It is a standard low-cost method suited to smaller lead paint jobs.

front: What respirator is commonly specified for lead work, and how is its filter identified?
back: PPE for lead work includes a properly fitted particulate respirator, commonly a P100 filter identified by its purple colour coding, along with disposable coveralls, gloves, and eye protection. This combination guards against both airborne lead dust and skin contact with debris.

front: What hygiene rule applies to workers inside a lead work containment area?
back: Workers must never eat, drink, or smoke inside a containment area, since doing so risks ingesting lead dust directly. They must wash their hands and face thoroughly before doing any of those things elsewhere on site.

front: How must lead-contaminated debris and used PPE from a job site be disposed of?
back: Lead-contaminated waste is regulated as hazardous waste in most Canadian jurisdictions above a defined threshold, so it cannot go into a regular bin. It must be double-bagged, labelled, and taken to a facility licensed for hazardous waste, and while provincial and municipal rules vary, this underlying obligation is constant across Canada.

front: How does the chapter distinguish mould from mildew?
back: Mould is a fungus that grows wherever there is moisture, an organic food source such as drywall paper or wood, and a survivable temperature range. Mildew is a related, more surface-level growth often seen on damp bathroom grout or shower walls, and both follow the same remediation logic.

front: What three conditions does mould require in order to grow?
back: Mould needs moisture, an organic food source such as drywall paper or wood, and a survivable temperature range. Removing any of these conditions, most practically the moisture, is central to stopping mould from coming back after remediation.

front: Why should a painter never simply paint over visible mould with a standard coating?
back: Painting over visible mould seals in moisture and feeds the fungus if the coating is not mould-resistant, guaranteeing the problem returns. The mould often bleeds straight through the new film rather than staying hidden.

front: How does the recommended response to mould differ between a small area and a larger contaminated area?
back: Small areas, generally under about one square metre, can often be handled directly with an N95 or better respirator, gloves, eye protection, and outside ventilation. Larger contaminated areas should go to a specialized remediation contractor, since extensive growth can signal a hidden moisture problem inside a wall cavity and may need containment with negative air pressure.

front: What is the correct sequence of steps for remediating a mould-affected area?
back: The sequence is to stop the moisture source, remove porous materials that cannot be fully cleaned such as water-damaged drywall, clean non-porous surfaces with an appropriate solution, let the area dry completely, then prime and repaint with a mould-resistant system. Following this order rather than skipping ahead is what makes the repair last.

front: What happens if the drying step is skipped during mould remediation?
back: Skipping the drying step is one of the most common and costly mistakes in mould remediation. Trapped moisture blisters the new coating and can restart mould growth beneath it, defeating the purpose of the repair.

front: Is mould-resistant paint a substitute for controlling the moisture source that caused the mould?
back: No. Prevention is about moisture control, not paint chemistry, through adequate exhaust ventilation, functioning vapour barriers, correct grading and drainage, and prompt leak repair. A mould-resistant paint or mildewcide additive helps in consistently damp areas but is not a substitute for fixing the actual moisture source.

front: What is the core skill behind drywall joint repair that makes a patch disappear once painted?
back: The core skill is building up joint compound in thin, progressively wider coats so the repair blends into the wall rather than showing as a hump or shadow line. Each successive coat must be thinner at its edges and wider than the coat beneath it.

front: What happens during the first coat of a taped drywall joint repair?
back: The first coat embeds paper or mesh tape into a bed of compound, pressed flat with a taping knife to squeeze out excess material and air bubbles. This bedding coat forms the foundation the wider coats will feather over.

front: How do the second and third coats of a taped drywall repair build on the first?
back: Once the first coat has cured, a second, wider coat goes over the tape, feathering the edges beyond the first coat's width so the buildup tapers gradually instead of ending in a ridge. A third finishing coat, wider again, feathers the repair out further, with light sanding between coats to knock down tool marks.

front: Define feathering in drywall repair, and explain why it is the most important concept in this section.
back: Feathering is the progressive widening of each joint compound coat so it extends further than the coat beneath it, thinning to nothing at its outer edge. It is the single most important concept in drywall repair, since a hand run across the dry, sanded repair should not be able to find where the patch ends.

front: How does a corner repair in drywall differ from a flat taped joint repair?
back: Corner repairs use the same layered feathering logic as a flat joint, but a paper-faced or metal corner bead keeps the angle straight. Compound is applied in the same progressively widening pattern on each side of the bead.

front: What repair materials are typically used for small holes versus larger holes in drywall?
back: Small holes are typically repaired with a self-adhesive mesh patch, while a rigid patch kit is used for larger holes. Both are then coated with the same progressively widening, feathered coats used on a taped joint.

front: Why can a technically excellent drywall repair still fail visually once painted?
back: Texture matching is where many otherwise solid drywall repairs fail visually, since a smooth, well-feathered patch on a textured wall will stand out under angled light even with perfect joint work. A painter needs to recognize the wall's existing texture and know how to reproduce it.

front: Describe the orange peel wall texture and its typical application method.
back: Orange peel is a light, stippled pattern resembling its namesake fruit. It is typically sprayed with a hopper gun using a thinned compound and moderate air pressure, producing small, even bumps.

front: Describe the knockdown wall texture and how it is created.
back: Knockdown starts as a heavier, splattered spray pattern with larger, randomly sized blobs. It is then lightly flattened with a wide knife or trowel while still wet, knocking down the peaks into flatter, mottled shapes.

front: What is popcorn, or acoustic, ceiling texture, and how was it historically applied?
back: Popcorn, or acoustic, texture is a heavier, three-dimensional ceiling texture, historically sprayed with polystyrene or vermiculite aggregate for a lumpy, sound-dampening surface. It was chosen for both its look and its sound-dampening function.

front: What safety concern applies specifically to popcorn ceilings installed before the 1980s?
back: Popcorn ceilings installed before the 1980s carry the same lead, and separately asbestos, screening concerns discussed elsewhere in the guide. Any repair on an older popcorn ceiling should be tested first, never assumed to be safe.

front: What is the recommended approach for matching an unfamiliar existing wall texture?
back: Matching an existing texture takes practice and, often, a test patch on scrap board first. Spray pattern, distance, air pressure, and compound thickness all affect the result, so these should be adjusted on the test area rather than the visible repair.

front: Why must a texture-matched drywall patch be primed before the final topcoat?
back: Once texture is matched and fully dry, the patch and a buffer area are primed before topcoating, because bare compound and older paint absorb paint differently. An unprimed patch will often flash through the finish coat as a dull or shiny spot.

front: What is parging, and what purpose does it serve on a foundation wall before coating?
back: Parging is a thin coat of cement-based mortar over concrete or masonry, most often applied to foundation walls. It smooths an uneven surface or restores a damaged section before painting or waterproofing.

front: How long should fresh parging be allowed to cure before it is painted, and why?
back: Fresh parging should generally cure for at least a week under good conditions before coating over it. Trapped moisture in fresh mortar blisters paint that is applied too early, so waiting protects the finished coating.

front: What is tuckpointing, and why should a painter recognize when it is needed?
back: Tuckpointing removes deteriorated mortar between bricks and replaces it, tooled to match the original joint profile. A painter should recognize failing joints as a sign that repointing is needed before any coating goes on, since painting over failing mortar traps moisture and accelerates the deterioration.

front: At roughly what point of mortar joint deterioration should a painter flag brick for repointing?
back: Mortar joints crumbling or receding more than roughly six millimetres from the brick face are a sign that repointing is needed before any coating work. Tuckpointing itself is specialized masonry work outside a painter's trade scope, but recognizing the need for it is not.

front: What is efflorescence, and how does it form on masonry or concrete surfaces?
back: Efflorescence is the white, powdery, salt-like deposit seen on masonry, concrete, or parging surfaces. It forms when water moving through the material dissolves soluble salts and carries them to the surface, where the water evaporates and leaves crystals behind.

front: Is efflorescence best understood as a cosmetic problem or as a moisture indicator?
back: Efflorescence is a moisture indicator first and a cosmetic problem second. Simply wire-brushing it off and painting without addressing the moisture source only brings it back, sometimes forcing the new paint film off the wall as salts keep migrating outward.

front: What is the correct sequence for treating an efflorescence-affected masonry surface?
back: The correct treatment is to dry-brush or wash off loose salts with plain water and a stiff brush, let the surface dry completely, and confirm the moisture source has been addressed. Only then should a masonry primer or sealer rated for high-pH, alkaline substrates be applied.

front: What is rust, and what causes it to form on metal surfaces?
back: Rust, or iron oxide, forms when ferrous metal meets oxygen and moisture over time. It is a corrosion process that affects iron-containing, or ferrous, metals specifically.

front: What happens if rust is left untreated underneath a paint coating?
back: Left untreated under a coating, rust keeps growing beneath the paint film, causing blistering, cracking, and eventual coating failure. This is why complete removal down to a sound substrate is non-negotiable before coating corroded metal.

front: When are hand tool methods appropriate for rust removal, and what do they involve?
back: Hand tool methods, including wire brushing, scraping, and hand sanding, suit light surface rust or small areas where power tools are impractical. They are slow but low-risk and require only basic PPE.

front: What power tools are used for rust removal, and what precautions do they require?
back: Power tool methods use a wire wheel, angle grinder with a flap disc, or needle scaler, removing rust and old coatings far faster than hand tools. They generate significant airborne dust and metal particulate, so eye and hearing protection plus a suitable respirator are required, and any old coating on a pre-1980 substrate should first be screened for lead.

front: How does a chemical rust converter work, and where is it most useful?
back: A rust converter chemically transforms iron oxide into a stable, paintable compound, commonly a black inert coating, rather than removing it physically. It is useful on pitted or hard-to-reach surfaces, but it works best on light to moderate rust and leaves a weaker long-term bond than a fully cleaned bare-metal surface.

front: What does abrasive blasting accomplish, and what is an anchor profile?
back: Abrasive blasting propels media such as steel grit, glass bead, or garnet at high velocity to strip rust, old coatings, and mill scale down to bare, profiled metal in one pass. Blasting produces an anchor profile, measured in thousandths of an inch or micrometres, which gives a new coating mechanical grip.

front: What does a phosphate treatment do to bare metal before priming?
back: A phosphate treatment, commonly iron or zinc phosphate, reacts with clean, bare metal to form a microscopically rough, corrosion-resistant crystalline layer. This slows new rust and improves primer adhesion, and is most common in shop and industrial settings.

front: What is the purpose of a conversion coating on metal, and is it a decorative finish?
back: Conversion coatings serve the same purpose as a phosphate treatment on bare or freshly blasted ferrous and non-ferrous metal alike. They are not a decorative finish but a prep step that measurably improves both corrosion resistance and adhesion before priming.

front: What preparation does a fibreglass surface need before painting, and what is the most common cause of failure?
back: Fibreglass surfaces are smooth and non-porous, so preparation means washing off wax, mould-release residue, or soap film, then scuff-sanding with a fine abrasive for a light mechanical profile before applying a bonding primer formulated for fibreglass or other slick plastics. Skipping the scuff-sand step is the most common cause of failure, since even a good paint peels quickly from a glass-smooth surface.

front: What preparation does plastic laminate, such as Arborite or Formica, need before painting?
back: Plastic laminate is a hard, non-porous, factory-finished surface that standard latex or alkyd paints will not bond to without prep. It should be cleaned of grease and residue, degloss-sanded with a fine grit abrasive, and coated with a bonding primer for slick substrates before any topcoat.

front: When is a chipped or delaminating section of plastic laminate beyond a coating repair?
back: Laminate that is chipped or delaminating at an edge is beyond a coating repair and should be flagged for replacement. No amount of bonding primer or surface prep restores the substrate once it has physically separated or broken away.

front: What must a painter check before recoating a previously coated industrial surface with an unknown coating history?
back: Compatibility between old and new coating systems is not automatic, since an incompatible new coating can cause lifting, wrinkling, or complete adhesion failure as its solvents attack the old film. Where the coating history is unknown, a test patch in an inconspicuous area, plus a lead check given the age typical of industrial infrastructure, is standard practice before full-scale prep and recoating.

front: What thickness of polyethylene sheeting is used for light dust control versus hazardous material containment?
back: Poly sheeting containment typically uses four-mil polyethylene for light dust control and six-mil for hazardous material work, taped continuously along floors, walls, and openings to seal off the work area. Seams should overlap generously and be taped fully, since gaps at seams and floor edges are the most common failure point.

front: How are doorways typically handled in a containment setup so workers can pass through safely?
back: Doorways are typically fitted with a zippered access flap or a two-stage vestibule, so workers can pass through the containment barrier without breaching it every time. This limits how often the seal is opened and reduces the chance of dust escaping.

front: How does negative air pressure containment work, and how is it verified on larger jobs?
back: A fan unit fitted with a HEPA filter continuously exhausts air from inside the containment faster than it can leak back in, creating lower pressure inside than outside so any airflow through small gaps moves inward. Negative air units are typically sized to a set number of air changes per hour, and on larger jobs a manometer may confirm the negative pressure is actually being held.

front: What are the four ingredient categories present in every paint formulation?
back: Every paint is a mixture of binder, pigment, solvent (also called the carrier), and additives. The binder forms the dry film and binds it to the substrate, pigment gives colour and hiding power, the solvent keeps everything workable until it evaporates or reacts away, and additives fine-tune performance in small percentages.

front: Why is the binder called the single biggest factor in a coating's durability?
back: The binder, or resin, is the glue that holds pigment particles together and sticks the dry film to the substrate. It is the main driver of flexibility, adhesion, and resistance to washing, UV light, and chemicals, which is why terms like 100% acrylic or alkyd describe the binder specifically.

front: What is the difference between a prime pigment and an extender pigment?
back: Prime pigments, most commonly titanium dioxide, provide colour and opacity to a paint film. Extender pigments, such as calcium carbonate or clay, add bulk and help control sheen without contributing much colour.

front: Why can a premium paint line hide better in fewer coats than an economy line using the same binder?
back: A premium line typically carries a higher ratio of prime pigment to extender pigment. More titanium dioxide relative to filler gives greater opacity per coat, so the premium product achieves full hide in fewer applications than an economy formulation diluted with more extender pigment.

front: What is the job of the solvent, or carrier, in a paint formulation?
back: The solvent keeps binder and pigment suspended and workable until the coating is applied. Its job is temporary, since it evaporates or reacts away as the film cures, leaving only binder and pigment behind as the dry film. Water is the carrier in water-based coatings, and an organic solvent such as mineral spirits is the carrier in solvent-based coatings.

front: Name three functions that additives commonly perform in a paint formulation.
back: Thickeners control viscosity and resist sagging, driers speed the oxidation reaction that cures oil and alkyd films, and biocides or mildewcides resist mould and bacterial growth. Coalescing agents are a fourth common additive, helping latex particles fuse together as the film dries.

front: Despite its name, does modern latex paint contain natural rubber?
back: No. Modern latex paint contains no natural rubber at all. The binder is almost always an acrylic or vinyl-acrylic polymer suspended as tiny particles in water, which is why the trade also calls this family of products water-based or acrylic coatings.

front: Describe coalescence, the cure mechanism of a latex or acrylic paint film.
back: Coalescence is a physical, not chemical, cure process. As water evaporates from the film, the suspended polymer particles are drawn together until they touch, deform, and fuse into a continuous film. Coalescing solvents in the formulation soften the particle surfaces enough to let this fusion happen at room temperature.

front: How long does latex paint take to dry to the touch versus reach full cure?
back: Latex paint typically dries to the touch within one to two hours. Full cure to final hardness, however, can take two to four weeks, so a freshly touch-dry latex surface is still vulnerable to marring or damage well after it feels dry.

front: List three strengths of acrylic latex coatings compared with oil-based coatings.
back: Acrylic coatings hold colour and gloss well because the polymer resists UV breakdown better than alkyd resin, and they stay flexible with substrate movement, reducing cracking. They also clean up with soap and water, carry low odour and low VOC content, and are breathable enough to let moisture vapour pass through, which matters on masonry and stucco.

front: Why can latex paint applied over a glossy or chalky surface fail to adhere properly?
