back: If a scratch or holiday exposes bare steel through a zinc rich primer, the surrounding zinc corrodes in preference to the steel because zinc is the more reactive metal. This sacrificial action keeps the exposed steel protected even though the film has a defect. It is the whole reason a zinc rich primer works differently from an ordinary barrier coating.

front: Compare inorganic and organic zinc rich primers.
back: Inorganic zinc primers use an inorganic binder, commonly a silicate, and require the zinc particles to be in direct metal to metal contact with each other and with the steel, so they demand a very clean, near-white or white metal blasted surface. They give outstanding long term protection but are less forgiving of marginal surface preparation and can be brittle underfoot on floors. Organic zinc primers use an organic resin binder, often an epoxy, and are more tolerant of imperfect surface preparation, easier to topcoat, and more flexible.

front: What surface preparation does an inorganic zinc primer demand, and why?
back: Inorganic zinc primers use a silicate binder and require the zinc particles to be in direct metal to metal contact with each other and with the steel to give galvanic protection. This means they demand a very clean, near-white or white metal blasted surface. Marginal surface preparation is much less forgiving for an inorganic zinc primer than for other coating types.

front: What zinc loading do zinc rich primers need, and why does it matter?
back: Inorganic zinc rich primers need a high zinc loading in the dry film, typically 80 to 95 percent by weight. Organic zinc rich primers run somewhat lower, typically 65 to 80 percent by weight, because their resin binder carries less zinc than an inorganic silicate binder can. A painter should recognize that zinc content, not just the presence of some zinc, is what makes the sacrificial protection work.

front: Why is a multi coat system specified as a package rather than as three products chosen separately?
back: Very little industrial steel work is protected by a single coat of anything, because each layer in a multi coat system has a distinct job. The primer, intermediate, and topcoat are engineered to work together, and each one is chosen and formulated to support the others. Choosing coats separately risks compatibility and performance problems the package approach avoids.

front: What is the job of the primer coat in a multi coat structural steel system?
back: The primer coat goes directly onto prepared steel and handles adhesion and, in many systems, corrosion inhibition. It bonds to the anchor profile created during abrasive blasting, giving the whole system its mechanical foundation. Everything else in the system depends on the primer being applied correctly to properly prepared steel.

front: What is the job of the intermediate coat, and why is it also called the build coat?
back: The intermediate coat, sometimes called the build coat, is the main contributor to overall film thickness and barrier protection. It is frequently a high build epoxy applied at a heavier thickness than most topcoats. It also hides minor holidays in the primer, adding a second, independent barrier layer, since a defect in one coat is unlikely to line up with a defect in the coat below it.

front: What determines the choice of topcoat in a multi coat structural steel system?
back: The topcoat is the final, visible layer, chosen for what the finished structure needs to show the world: colour, gloss, UV stability, and resistance to the exposure the structure will face. On a structure exposed to sunlight this is very often a polyurethane. Other topcoat chemistries can be selected to suit specialized chemical exposure instead.

front: Describe a common zinc, epoxy, urethane system used on structural steel.
back: A common example on structural steel pairs a zinc rich primer, an epoxy intermediate coat, and a polyurethane topcoat, often shortened to a zinc, epoxy, urethane system. Each coat carries a target dry film thickness, and the system's total thickness is what actually sets the service life estimate. This combination gives galvanic protection, barrier build, and UV stable colour in one package.

front: What can happen if a painter skips a coat or applies coats too thin in a multi coat system?
back: Painters must apply every coat in the right order, at the right thickness, and within the specified recoat window. Skipping a coat, applying coats too thin, or letting too much time pass between coats can compromise intercoat adhesion and shorten real world performance. This can happen even though the finished job might look fine on completion day.

front: Which two organizations publish the surface preparation standards used across North America, and what do they operate as together?
back: The standards most often referenced were jointly published by SSPC, originally the Society for Protective Coatings, and NACE. The two now operate together as AMPP, the Association for Materials Protection and Performance. A painter on industrial jobs will see these standards called out by name on a spec sheet.

front: Why do industrial specifications call out a written surface preparation standard instead of a general description?
back: Surface preparation matters more in industrial work than almost anywhere else in the trade, because these coating systems depend on strong, uniform adhesion to perform for years under harsh exposure. Rather than a vague description like clean and sand, a written standard has a defined visual appearance. A prepared surface can then be checked against photographs and written criteria instead of being left to judgment.

front: Describe white metal blast cleaning and where it is specified.
back: White metal blast cleaning is the most aggressive surface preparation standard, removing all visible rust, mill scale, old coating, and contamination from the entire surface. It leaves a uniform metallic colour across 100 percent of the surface. It is specified for the most demanding immersion service, such as tank linings, where any residual contamination could undermine the coating.

front: How does near-white metal blast cleaning differ from white metal blast cleaning, and where is it commonly used?
back: Near-white metal blast cleaning is slightly less exacting than white metal, allowing very light, random staining to remain on around 5 percent of the surface. It is one of the most common specifications for structural steel systems, including a zinc, epoxy, urethane system. It delivers excellent adhesion without the extra cost of a full white metal finish.

front: What is commercial blast cleaning, and when is it suited?
back: Commercial blast cleaning permits staining to remain on up to around a third of the surface. It suits a less severe service environment where a lower cost preparation is acceptable, rather than an immersion or highly corrosive exposure. It sits between near-white metal blast cleaning and the lighter brush-off standard.

front: What is brush-off blast cleaning, and what kind of work is it used for?
back: Brush-off blast cleaning is the lightest surface preparation standard, mainly removing loose material and slightly roughening the surface. It is used for lighter duty maintenance coating rather than a demanding new construction system. It leaves far more of the original surface condition in place than the heavier blast standards.

front: When would a painter use hand tool or power tool cleaning instead of abrasive blasting?
back: Hand tool cleaning and power tool cleaning are non-abrasive-blast standards used where blasting is not practical, such as occupied sites or spot repairs. Hand tool cleaning uses wire brushes, scrapers, and sandpaper worked by hand. Power tool cleaning uses powered wire brushes, needle guns, grinders, or sanding discs to do the same job faster and to a cleaner standard.

front: Why is sand rarely used as an abrasive blasting media today?
back: Sand was historically a common abrasive blasting media, but it is now heavily restricted in many jurisdictions because of the silicosis hazard from breathing fine silica dust. A painter should expect to see it rarely and only under strict controls. Other media have largely replaced it in modern industrial blasting practice.

front: Compare steel grit and steel shot as abrasive blasting media.
back: Steel grit and steel shot are widely used on structural steel, with grit producing a sharper profile than the rounder profile produced by shot. Both are recyclable through blast pot recovery systems, which makes them economical on large jobs. The choice between them depends on the anchor profile shape the specification requires.

front: What are coal slag and specialty media used for in abrasive blasting?
back: Coal slag and other mineral slag abrasives are common single use media offering a good angular profile at lower cost than recyclable steel media. Specialty media such as garnet or plastic and organic media suit sensitive substrates or jobs where minimizing dust matters. Media selection depends on the substrate, the required finish, and site restrictions.

front: What is an anchor profile, and what job does it do?
back: An anchor profile is a controlled roughness on the steel surface created by abrasive blasting, measured in mils. It gives the coating film mechanical adhesion in addition to any chemical bond. This mechanical grip is a key reason industrial coatings need blasted steel rather than a simply cleaned surface.

front: What is the typical anchor profile depth range, and how is it checked?
back: Profile depth is specified as a range, commonly between 1.5 and 4 mils, and is checked with profile comparator gauges or replica tape. A profile too shallow reduces mechanical adhesion, while a profile too deep can leave peaks poking through a thin coat. Hitting the specified range matters as much as simply roughing up the steel.

front: What is wet film thickness (WFT) and when is it checked?
back: Wet film thickness is checked immediately after application, while the coating is still liquid, using a wet film gauge. Checking WFT lets a painter correct technique on the spot, before the coating cures, rather than finding out afterward that a section was applied too thin. It is a real time quality check during application.

front: Describe how a wet film gauge is used to read wet film thickness.
back: A wet film gauge is typically a small notched comb that is pressed into the wet film and lifted straight out. The wettest notch that still shows paint tells the applicator roughly how thick the film is at that moment. This simple mechanical check gives an immediate reading without waiting for the coating to cure.

front: Why does wet film thickness read higher than the eventual dry film thickness?
back: Wet coatings shrink as solvent leaves the film during cure, so wet readings run higher than the eventual dry reading. Experienced applicators know roughly what wet reading to aim for to land on the dry target. This relationship is why WFT is a useful on the spot check but DFT remains the measurement that actually matters.

front: Why is dry film thickness (DFT) considered the measurement that actually matters?
back: Dry film thickness reflects the true, cured thickness after solvents have evaporated or the reaction has completed, which is what the coating's actual performance depends on. DFT is measured with a magnetic pull off gauge on steel or with electronic gauges. Readings are taken across the job in a specified pattern so average thickness and any thin spots are documented.

front: What problems result from a dry film that is too thin?
back: A film too thin will not deliver the corrosion or chemical resistance the system was designed to provide, since barrier protection depends on adequate film build. For a zinc primer, galvanic protection also depends on adequate film build. A thin film can look complete on the surface while failing to meet its actual performance requirement.

front: What problems can result from a dry film that is applied too thick?
back: A film too thick can cause its own problems, including trapped solvent or reaction byproducts leading to solvent popping, pinholing, wrinkling, or cracking as the coating shrinks and stresses build within it. This is why every specified system carries both a minimum and a maximum dry film thickness. A painter's job is to land inside that range coat by coat, not just to hit a total average.

front: Why must a painter hit the specified DFT range on every individual coat, not just the total average?
back: Every specified system carries a minimum and a maximum dry film thickness, and a painter's job is to land inside that range coat by coat. Hitting only an overall average across the whole system could still leave one coat too thin or too thick even if the total looks correct. Per coat control is what protects the system's intended performance.

front: Why are industrial coatings almost always sprayed rather than brushed or rolled?
back: Industrial coatings are almost always sprayed for productivity on large surfaces and because spraying gives more consistent, controllable film build across a big structure. Brushing or rolling would be far slower and less uniform on the scale of a tank, bridge, or large steel structure. Spray application is the standard method across industrial coating work.

front: What is plural component (proportioning) spray equipment, and what is it used for?
back: Plural component equipment draws each component of a two component product from its own separate pump and feed line, proportions the two streams to the correct mix ratio, and mixes them right at the gun tip rather than in a pot beforehand. It is built for products like epoxy, polyurethane, and especially fast curing polyurea. This lets a crew spray a product with a very short pot life, including a polyurea that would gel in seconds if hand mixed.

front: What features do plural component spray rigs typically include to keep the mix ratio on target?
back: Plural component rigs typically include heated hose packages to improve flow of the coating through the lines. They also include ratio monitoring so an operator can confirm the mix stays on target through the job. These features support consistent, correctly proportioned coating even on a long spray run.

front: When is conventional airless spray equipment used instead of plural component equipment?
back: Conventional airless spray equipment remains the standard tool for high build coatings that do not require plural component proportioning, particularly two component products with a workable pot life that can be pot mixed by hand before loading. It atomizes coating by forcing it through a small tip opening at very high hydraulic pressure rather than mixing it with compressed air. This lets it apply thick, high build films efficiently, an important advantage where a single coat is often several times the thickness of a typical architectural coat.

front: Define a confined space in the context of industrial coating work.
back: A confined space is generally an area large enough for a worker to enter and work in, with limited or restricted entry or exit, not designed for continuous human occupancy. Tanks, vessels, and silos are common confined spaces in industrial coating work. This basic definition brings a distinct set of hazards into a painter's daily work that residential and commercial painting almost never involves.

front: What hazards does coating work inside a tank or vessel add to the basic confined space definition?
back: Solvent vapours can accumulate in a poorly ventilated confined space and create both a health hazard through inhalation and a fire or explosion hazard if vapour concentration reaches a flammable range. Oxygen levels inside a sealed vessel can also be displaced or depleted. These hazards are on top of the basic restricted entry and exit problem of any confined space.

front: What must be in place before a painter enters a tank or vessel to spray coatings?
back: Confined space entry for coating work always requires atmospheric testing before and during entry, forced ventilation to keep vapour and oxygen levels within safe limits, and a documented entry permit system with an attendant stationed outside and a rescue plan in place. A painter should never enter a tank or vessel to spray coatings without confirming that permit, ventilation, and monitoring are active. This applies no matter how routine the job seems.

front: What is holiday testing, and what does it detect?
back: Holiday testing uses an electrical device, a low voltage wet sponge tester for thinner films or a high voltage spark tester for thicker films, to detect holidays: pinholes, thin spots, or other tiny discontinuities that would otherwise let moisture or chemicals reach the substrate undetected. A holiday invisible to the eye can still complete an electrical circuit through the gap in the film, so the tester finds defects visual inspection alone would miss. It is a key inspection check on critical systems, particularly tank linings and buried or immersed steel.

front: What is a recoat window, and why is it temperature dependent?
back: The recoat window is the range of time after one coat is applied during which the next coat can go on and still achieve full intercoat adhesion. Recoating too soon can lift or disturb the first coat, while waiting too long past the maximum window can let the first coat cure so completely that the next coat has nothing to bond to, sometimes requiring re-abrading before proceeding. Because two component coatings cure by chemical reaction, recoat times are temperature dependent, with cold temperatures extending the window and hot temperatures compressing it.

front: What four elements must be present at the same time for corrosion to occur?
back: Corrosion needs an anode, a cathode, an electrolyte, and a metallic path connecting them, since it is an electrochemical reaction running as a circuit. Removing any one of the four stops the reaction. This is why controlling moisture, the electrolyte, is such an effective way to slow corrosion.

front: What is the anode in a corrosion cell, and what happens there?
back: The anode is the site on the metal that gives up electrons and goes into solution as ions, and it is the area that actually corrodes. On unprotected steel, iron leaving the metal at anodic sites combines with oxygen to form rust. The cathode, by contrast, does not lose metal.

front: What is the cathode in a corrosion cell, and does it corrode?
back: The cathode is the site where electrons released at the anode are consumed, usually by reacting with oxygen and water to form hydroxide ions. The cathode does not lose metal, which is the whole principle behind forcing a structure to become the cathode for protection. It can be a separate area on the same piece of steel or a different metal in contact with it.

front: What role does the electrolyte play in a corrosion cell?
back: The electrolyte is any conductive liquid film that lets ions move between the anode and the cathode, such as rainwater or, faster still, water carrying dissolved salts. Without an electrolyte present, the corrosion circuit cannot complete and the reaction stops. This is why moisture control is the single biggest lever for slowing corrosion.

front: What is the metallic path in a corrosion cell?
back: The metallic path is the physical connection between the anode and the cathode that lets electrons flow between them. On a single piece of steel, the steel itself serves as this path. All four elements, anode, cathode, electrolyte, and metallic path, must exist together for corrosion to proceed.

front: Why can steel rust inside a covered, unheated warehouse even though it looks dry?
back: Steel does not need to look wet to corrode. A microscopic film of moisture from ordinary humidity is enough to act as the electrolyte and complete the corrosion circuit. This is why indoor structural steel in an unheated space can still develop rust over time.

front: What is galvanic corrosion, and which metal is affected?
back: Galvanic corrosion occurs when two dissimilar metals with different electrical potentials touch in the presence of an electrolyte, building an anode and cathode pair directly into the structure. The less noble metal becomes the anode and corrodes faster, while the more noble metal is protected. A steel rail bolted to a stainless bracket turns the steel into the anode, since stainless is more noble than mild steel, while steel screws fastening aluminum flashing turn the aluminum into the anode instead, since aluminum is less noble than steel.

front: Besides moisture and galvanic contact, what other conditions accelerate corrosion?
back: Salts make moisture far more conductive, which is why steel near the ocean or exposed to de-icing salt spray needs heavier protection than similar steel inland. Temperature, mechanical stress that cracks a protective film, and contamination from welding, oil, or chlorides all add to corrosion rate as well, and these factors rarely act alone.

front: What is the basic principle behind cathodic protection?
back: Since corrosion only happens at anodic sites and a cathode does not corrode, a structure can be protected by forcing it to become the cathode of a circuit instead. Coatings are the first line of defence against corrosion, but many structures pair them with a cathodic protection system as backup. Painters do not design or install these systems but need to understand how they interact with the coating.

front: How does a sacrificial anode system provide cathodic protection?
back: A sacrificial anode system connects a more reactive metal, such as zinc, aluminum, or magnesium, to the steel within the same electrolyte. Being less noble than steel, that metal becomes the anode of the combined circuit and corrodes away in the steel's place. The anodes are designed to wear out and be replaced on a set schedule.

front: How does an impressed current system differ from a sacrificial anode system?
back: An impressed current system uses an external power source, a rectifier, to push direct current onto the structure through separate anodes placed nearby, rather than relying on a sacrificial metal that wears away. This lets an operator control and monitor protection electronically across much larger structures. It is typically used where a sacrificial system alone would not provide enough capacity.

front: How do coatings and cathodic protection work together on a protected structure?
back: A good coating reduces the exposed surface area of bare steel, so a smaller cathodic protection system can cover the whole structure. Coating failures, on the other hand, increase current demand and can overload the protection system. The two are meant to function as a combined defence, not as independent backups.

front: What special resistance property must coatings used with cathodic protection have?
back: Coatings meant to work with cathodic protection must resist cathodic disbondment, a failure where the protective current itself causes the coating to lose adhesion near a holiday in the film. This is a specialized requirement beyond ordinary adhesion performance. Pipeline and submerged tank coatings in particular are tested specifically for this resistance.

front: On what types of structures will a painter typically encounter cathodic protection systems?
back: Cathodic protection is commonly found on buried pipelines, tank bottoms, ship hulls, and offshore platforms. Painters do not design or install these systems, but their coating work must be compatible with the cathodic protection already in place or planned for the structure.

front: What are the three exposure zones a single marine piling can pass through?
back: A marine piling can pass through the atmospheric zone, the splash zone, and the submerged zone all on one structure, and each demands different protection. This is what makes marine and offshore coating specification unusually complex compared to a single uniform exposure. The splash zone is consistently the most aggressive of the three.

front: Describe the atmospheric zone on a marine structure.
back: The atmospheric zone sits above the highest wave and spray reach. It corrodes faster than an equivalent inland structure due to constant salt exposure, but it dries between wettings and is relatively easy to inspect compared to the other two zones.

front: Why is the splash zone the most aggressive corrosion zone on a marine structure?
back: The splash zone is alternately wetted by waves and spray, then dried by air and sun, roughly straddling the high tide line up through spray reach. Repeated wetting and drying constantly delivers fresh oxygen to the surface, feeding the cathode reaction, while wave action abrades the film. Splash zone steel can corrode several times faster than submerged steel on the same structure.

front: Why are splash zone coating systems typically the thickest specified on a marine structure?
back: The splash zone is hard to maintain because it is difficult to keep dry long enough for proper surface preparation, and it experiences the fastest corrosion rate on the structure. Splash zone systems are often glass flake reinforced epoxies, chosen to resist abrasion from wave action as well as corrosion.

front: How does corrosion in the submerged zone compare to the splash zone?
back: In the submerged zone, oxygen must diffuse through standing water to reach the steel, which slows corrosion compared to the splash zone, though it is still faster than dry atmospheric exposure. This zone is where cathodic protection does its heaviest work, paired with a coating rated for continuous immersion.

front: What do antifouling coatings do, and how does that differ from corrosion protection?
back: Antifouling coatings prevent or slow marine organisms such as barnacles, algae, and mussels from growing on submerged surfaces, since unchecked fouling adds significant drag to a hull and raises fuel use. Their job has nothing to do with corrosion, which is why antifouling topcoats always go over a separate anticorrosive primer rather than protecting the steel themselves.

front: What is the difference between traditional and foul release antifouling coatings?
back: Traditional antifouling coatings slowly release a biocide, historically a copper compound, to deter marine growth. Modern foul release coatings instead use a low friction silicone surface that organisms cannot grip onto in the first place. Both categories still require a separate anticorrosive primer underneath.

front: What must water storage tank linings be certified for on potable reservoirs?
back: Water storage tank linings used on potable reservoirs and fire protection tanks must be certified safe for drinking water contact under the applicable standard. A general industrial coating that resists corrosion well should never be assumed acceptable for potable service without that certification. Cure time also matters, since a lining returned to service too soon can leach taste or odour before it fully cures.

front: Why do fuel storage tank linings often need a conductive or static dissipative additive?
back: Moving fuel can generate static electricity, and an insulating film could let that charge build with no path to ground. Inside a vessel holding flammable vapour, that is a spark hazard, so fuel tank linings are commonly specified with a conductive or static dissipative additive in addition to hydrocarbon chemical resistance.

front: What must fuel storage tank linings resist beyond static buildup?
back: Fuel storage tank linings need chemical resistance to hydrocarbons and must stay adherent through repeated fill and empty cycles as the tank goes from full to empty and back. Losing adhesion under these cycles would expose bare steel to the fuel and moisture inside the tank.

front: How is a chemical storage tank lining selected?
back: Chemical storage tank linings are selected based on exactly what chemical the tank holds, at what concentration and temperature, since different resins resist different chemical families. A lining that performs perfectly in a caustic tank can fail rapidly in an acidic one. The owner's compatibility chart and the manufacturer's data sheet govern the choice, never general similarity between products.

front: Why is there no practical way to touch up a tank lining after the tank returns to service?
back: Once a tank is back in service and full of product, its interior lining cannot practically be inspected or repaired. This is why surface preparation and film thickness control matter even more on interior tank work than on exterior steel work, where a missed spot can still be found and fixed later.

front: What type of work does interior tank lining application almost always involve?
back: Interior tank work is almost always confined space work, since a tank interior is large enough to enter, has limited means of entry or exit, and is not designed for continuous occupancy. This means confined space entry procedures apply on top of the coating specification itself.

front: What is the purpose of fireproofing on structural steel?
back: Structural steel loses strength rapidly as it heats in a fire and can fail within minutes of direct exposure, well before a fire might otherwise be controlled. Fireproofing exists to keep steel below its critical failure temperature long enough for evacuation and emergency response, buying time rather than preventing the fire itself.

front: What advantage do intumescent coatings have over sprayed cementitious or mineral fibre fireproofing?
back: Intumescent coatings protect steel while letting it keep its finished architectural appearance, which sprayed cementitious or mineral fibre fireproofing cannot offer. Under normal conditions an intumescent coating looks and behaves like ordinary paint, applied at a controlled dry film thickness over an appropriate primer and often finished with a topcoat.

front: What happens to an intumescent coating when it is exposed to fire temperatures?
back: The chemistry only activates at fire temperatures, when the film expands dramatically, swelling to many times its original thickness in a process called intumescence. This forms a thick, stable char full of tiny gas pockets. Trapped gas conducts heat far more slowly than a solid material, so the char slows heat transfer into the steel.

front: What fire rating periods are commonly specified for intumescent coating systems?
back: Intumescent coating systems commonly hold steel below its critical temperature for a rated period of 30, 60, 90, or 120 minutes. That rated period is earned by the specific combination of primer, film thickness, coat count, and topcoat tested together as one system in a laboratory.

front: Where are intumescent coatings typically specified on a building?
back: Intumescent coatings are specified on columns, beams, and connections where the structural frame needs a fire rating and the design also calls for exposed, architecturally finished steel. This combination is common in atriums, open plan interiors, and parking structures.

front: Why must applicators follow the manufacturer's intumescent coating system exactly?
back: The specified primer, film thickness, coat count, and topcoat all belong to a combination that earned its fire rating in a laboratory test, as an engineered and certified assembly. Substituting a different primer or applying less thickness than specified can invalidate the rating even if the job looks fine, since dry film thickness measurement is the entire basis for whether the system performs in a real fire.

front: How does a negative pressure enclosure control contamination during blasting?
back: A negative pressure enclosure is built with tarps, scaffolding, and sealed framing, and a ventilation system continuously pulls air out through filtration rather than pushing air in, creating slightly negative pressure inside relative to outside. Any small gaps then draw outside air in rather than letting contaminated dust leak out. The same exhaust also removes dust and overspray from the workers' breathing zone, working alongside personal respiratory protection rather than replacing it.

front: What is debris containment, and why does it matter on bridge and marine work?
back: Debris containment catches spent abrasive and paint chips at the base of the structure using ground tarps, catch platforms, or full enclosures depending on job size. On bridge and marine work, keeping this material out of the water below is often a hard regulatory requirement, not just good practice.

front: When must spent abrasive be tested and disposed of as hazardous waste?
back: Abrasive that removed an old lead based coating, common on older industrial and bridge structures, picks up that contamination and must be tested and handled as hazardous waste past regulatory thresholds, through a licensed facility. The coating history of the structure determines whether this applies.

front: When can spent abrasive be handled as ordinary construction waste?
back: Abrasive from bare steel or modern coatings with no legacy contamination can often be handled as ordinary construction waste. It should never be assumed safe without testing, however, whenever a structure's coating history is unknown.

front: What is delamination, and what commonly causes it?
back: Delamination is loss of adhesion between coating layers, or between coating and substrate, causing the film to lift, peel, or flake in sheets. Typical causes include inadequate surface preparation that left contamination or mill scale, applying a coat outside the recoat window so the bond never formed, or coating over a surface contaminated with oil, salt, or moisture.

front: What are holidays in a coating, and why are they dangerous?
back: Holidays, also called pinholes, are small gaps or discontinuities where the substrate is inadequately covered. They typically result from insufficient film thickness, trapped air bubbles that later broke, poor technique around edges and welds, or a film sagging away from sharp edges. Holidays are dangerous because they are often invisible to the eye, which is why holiday testing exists as a dedicated inspection step.

front: What causes under film corrosion, and why does it produce a blister larger than the original defect?
back: Under film corrosion happens when moisture and oxygen reach the substrate through a holiday, scratch, or porous area, and corrosion begins beneath an otherwise intact looking film. Because rust takes up more volume than the original steel, it pushes the film up from underneath, often creating a blister well beyond the size of the original defect.

front: What is cathodic disbondment?
back: Cathodic disbondment is a specialized failure on structures under cathodic protection. At a holiday where bare steel is exposed and simultaneously receiving protective current, the reaction generates hydroxide ions and can raise the local pH significantly, attacking the bond at the edges of the defect. This causes the coating to lose adhesion and spread outward from the holiday, even though the steel underneath is being protected.

front: Why are pipeline and submerged tank coatings tested specifically for disbondment resistance?
back: Cathodic disbondment is a failure mode unique to coatings on cathodically protected structures, so general adhesion testing alone will not reveal a coating's vulnerability to it. Pipeline and submerged tank coatings are therefore tested specifically for disbondment resistance, since these structures commonly rely on cathodic protection.

front: What does holiday testing find, and why is it also called spark testing?
back: Holiday testing finds pinholes and thin spots in a coating that are not visible to the eye. It is sometimes called spark testing because the high voltage version of the test produces a visible arc, or spark, at any holiday it detects.

front: How does a low voltage wet sponge holiday detector work?
back: A sponge electrode wetted with a low voltage detergent solution is passed over the coated surface, connected to a ground on the bare substrate. Where a holiday exposes the substrate, the circuit completes and the detector alarms. Wet sponge detectors are used on thinner films, generally up to around 500 micrometres.

front: How does a high voltage holiday detector work, and when is it used?
back: A wire brush or conductive rubber electrode passes over the surface at much higher voltage than a wet sponge detector, and at a holiday the voltage arcs through the thin remaining film, triggering an alarm. High voltage detectors are used on thicker films, common on heavy duty tank linings and pipeline coatings.

front: Why must holiday detector voltage be calibrated to the actual film thickness?
back: Too low a voltage setting can miss real holidays that exist in a thicker film, while too high a setting can punch through good film and create new pinholes that were not there before testing. Calibrating voltage to the actual measured film thickness avoids both errors.

front: How does pull off adhesion testing work?
back: Pull off testing glues a dolly to the coated surface and a calibrated tester pulls it straight away, measuring the tensile force needed to detach the coating. It also identifies where the failure occurred, whether at the substrate, between coats, or within a single coat layer.

front: How does cross hatch adhesion testing differ from pull off testing?
back: Cross hatch testing scores a grid of small squares through the film to the substrate, then applies and removes tape over the grid, rating how much coating pulled away versus stayed bonded. It is more common on thinner shop and field coatings than pull off testing, which is used on heavier systems.

front: What defines a confined space on a coating job?
back: A confined space is large enough to enter and work in, has limited means of entry or exit, and is not designed for continuous occupancy, such as a tank interior or an enclosed structural void. These spaces can develop oxygen deficient or enriched atmospheres and trap flammable or toxic vapour from solvent based coatings with no natural ventilation.

front: What must happen before entering a confined space to apply coatings?
back: The atmosphere must be tested for oxygen level, flammability, and toxic contaminants before entry, and the space must be continuously ventilated, monitored, and worked under a permit system with an attendant outside and a rescue plan in place. An untested, unpermitted confined space must never be entered regardless of schedule pressure.

front: Why do isocyanate containing polyurethane coatings require specific respiratory protection?
back: Isocyanates are among the most aggressive respiratory sensitizers in the trade, and two component polyurethane and polyurea coatings release isocyanate vapour and, when spray applied, isocyanate containing aerosol. A single significant exposure can sensitize a worker's respiratory system permanently, after which even tiny future exposures can trigger a severe asthma like reaction, so spray application requires supplied air respiratory protection, not a cartridge respirator.

front: What respiratory hazards does ventilation control during blasting and spraying?
back: Mechanical ventilation, whether through negative pressure containment or standalone forced air, protects workers from silica dust generated by certain blast media, general abrasive dust, and solvent vapour and overspray. It must keep contaminant levels within safe limits in the workers' actual breathing zone, and respirator selection follows the exposure assessment and safety data sheet, not habit or convenience.

front: What key elements does a typical industrial coating specification identify?
back: A specification identifies the required surface preparation standard by name and grade, states the primer, intermediate, and topcoat products by manufacturer and name, and specifies dry film thickness for each coat and for the total system. It also sets environmental limits and required testing such as holiday testing, adhesion testing, and film thickness verification.

front: What is the recoat window in a coating specification, and why does it matter?
back: The recoat window is the minimum and maximum time allowed between coats for proper intercoat adhesion. Applying a coat outside that window, either too soon or too late, is one of the common causes of delamination, since the bond between coats never forms properly.

front: What is the correct response if a specification appears wrong for the actual service conditions?
back: The correct response is to raise the concern with the specifier or engineer of record in writing before proceeding. The products, thicknesses, and environmental limits in a specification are the tested and approved system, so quietly substituting a different product or thickness, even one that seems equivalent, can void a warranty or fail an inspection outright.
